## Overview

In this graded assignment, you will practice primarily with Slurm batch jobs.
In the last part, you will also use generative AI to help you with one of the
questions --- and critically evaluate what it tells you.

::: callout-warning
#### Assumed knowledge
This assignment assumes that you have done the
[week 8 exercises](../week08/w8_exercises.qmd),
which introduced and used TrimGalore.
If you didn't do these already,
we strongly recommend you do so before attempting to do this assignment.
:::

## Directions and grading

### Submission expectations

- **Deadline**: Sunday Oct 25^th^ at 11:59 pm.
- **Submission**: You will submit your assignment by tagging the instructor in an
  Issue in your GitHub as per the last step below.

### Academic integrity

::: callout-important
### Gen-AI check

**This is the first assignment in which you are allowed to use generative AI.**
Now that we've covered these tools in week 8,
the course guideline from here on
(including for the Final Project) applies:

- You may use genAI, **as long as you can explain what your code does**.
  If genAI produces commands or constructs that we have not covered in class,
  do the research needed to understand them ---
  you may be asked to explain your code live over Zoom.
- Whatever the source, **you remain responsible for whether the code is correct**.
  "The AI told me so" is not a defense for a wrong answer,
  and as you'll see in Part D, it is quite capable of inventing options that
  don't exist.
- In Part D, you are **required** to document your genAI usage.
  Elsewhere in the assignment, documenting it is optional but encouraged.

Getting help from other people, and collaborating, are still not permitted.
:::

## Detailed steps

### Part A: Setting up & Git

1. Start a VS Code session at OSC in the folder `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER`.
   Create a new dir for this assignment, `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER/GA4`,
   and switch to that folder in VS Code using the "Open Folder" option.
   _This should be your working dir for the entire assignment._

2. Initialize a Git repository.
   Commit to the repo throughout the assignment as you see fit,
   but at least once for each "Part" of this assignment.
   Use and commit a `.gitignore` file as appropriate.
   _(Tip: Many of you would do well to recall the feedback you got_
   _on your Git repo from the previous assignment!)_

3. Inside dir `GA4`, create a `README.md` file and open it in the VS Code editor.
   Use this file throughout the assigment to add your answers where appropriate.

4. Inside dir `GA4`, also create dirs `scripts` and `results`.
   We'll make your dir self-contained again
   (like a typical situation for a research project)
   by copying some data into it:

   ```bash
   # (This command will work as intended if you *don't* have a data dir yet)
   cp -rv ../garrigos/fastq data
   ```

5. As a starting script, store the code below in a shell script `scripts/trimgalore.sh`.
   This is a script to run TrimGalore, which should be very similar to your final
   script from [last week's exercises](../week08/w8_exercises.qmd).

   ```bash
   #!/bin/bash
   set -euo pipefail

   # Constants
   TRIMGALORE_CONTAINER=oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/trim-galore:0.6.10--bc38c9238980c80e

   # Copy the placeholder variables
   R1="$1"
   R2="$2"
   outdir="$3"

   # Report
   echo "# Starting script trimgalore.sh"
   date
   echo "# Input R1 FASTQ file:      $R1"
   echo "# Input R2 FASTQ file:      $R2"
   echo "# Output dir:               $outdir"
   echo

   # Create the output dir
   mkdir -p "$outdir"

   # Run TrimGalore
   apptainer exec "$TRIMGALORE_CONTAINER" \
       trim_galore \
       --paired \
       --fastqc \
       --output_dir "$outdir" \
       "$R1" \
       "$R2"

   # Report
   echo
   echo "# TrimGalore version:"
   apptainer exec "$TRIMGALORE_CONTAINER" \
     trim_galore -v
   echo "# Successfully finished script trimgalore.sh"
   date
   ```

### Part B: A TrimGalore batch job

You'll start with the TrimGalore script you just created, which should be much
like that from last week's exercises.
But this time, instead of running the TrimGalore script "directly" with `bash`,
you will submit it as a batch job.
Then, in the next section,
you will submit many batch jobs at the same time: one for each sample.

06. Add Sbatch options to the top of the TrimGalore shell script to specify:

    - The account/project you want to use
    - The number of cores you want to reserve: use 8
    - The amount of time you want to reserve: use 30 minutes
    - The desired file name of Slurm log file
    - That Slurm should email you upon job failure
    - _Optional: you can try other Sbatch options you'd like to test_

07. By printing and scanning through the TrimGalore help info once again
    (see last week's exercises),
    find the TrimGalore option that specifies how many cores it can use --
    add the relevant line(s) from the TrimGalore help info to your `README.md`.
    In the script, change the `trim_galore` command accordingly to use the available
    number of cores.

08. To test the script and batch job submission,
    submit the script as a batch job only for sample `S63`.

09. Monitor the job, and when it's done, check that everything went well
    (if it didn't, redo until you get it right).
    In your `README.md`, explain your monitoring and checking process.
    Then, remove all outputs (Slurm log files and TrimGalore output files)
    produced by this test-run.

10. Illumina sequencing uses colors to distinguish between nucleotides
    as they are being added during the sequencing-by-synthesis process.
    However, newer Illumina machines (Nextseq and Novaseq) use a different color
    chemistry than older ones, and this newer chemistry suffers from an artefact
    that can erroneously produce strings of `G`s ("poly-G") with high quality scores.
    Those `G`s should really be `N`s instead,
    and occur especially at the end of reverse (R2) reads.

    In the FastQC outputs for the R2 file that you just produced with TrimGalore
    (recall that it runs FastQC after trimmming!),
    do you see any evidence for this problem? Explain.

11. We'll assume that the data was indeed produced with the newer Illumina
    color chemistry.
    In the TrimGalore help info, find the relevant TrimGalore option to deal with
    the poly-G problem,
    and again add the relevant line(s) from the help info to your `README.md`.
    Then, use the TrimGalore option you found,
    but don't change the quality score threshold from the default.

12. Rerun TrimGalore with the added color-chemistry option.
    Check all outputs and confirm that usage of this option made a difference.
    Then, remove all outputs produced by this test-run again.

### Bonus: Modify the script to rename the output FASTQ files

_If you choose not to do this Bonus part, you can simply move on to Part C._

The TrimGalore output FASTQ files are oddly named,
ending in `_R1_val_1.fq.gz` and `_R2_val_2.fq.gz` --
check the output files from your initial run to see this.
This is not _necessarily_ a problem,
but could trip you up in a next step with these files.

Therefore, modify your TrimGalore script to rename the output files after running
TrimGalore, giving them the same names as the input files.
Then, rerun the script to check that your changes were successful.

<details><summary>Hints _(Click to expand)_</summary>

To rename the files,
you first need to extract and store the part of the file name that is basically
a sample ID: that before `_R1.fastq.gz`/`_R2.fastq.gz`.
To do that, you will need to use "command substitution" and the `basename` command.
Those were explained on the "Unix shell tips and tricks" (week 7 - Lecture C) page
[starting here](../week07/w7c_tricks.qmd#command-substitution) but we did not
cover them together in class.

Here is a skeleton of the code to extract that part of the file name:

```bash
# Replace " ... " with your code.
sample_id=$( ... )
```

Based on that ID, you can build up the names of the TrimGalore output files
_and_ those of the desired final file names. For example:

```bash
# The name of the initial ('init') TrimGalore R1 output file will be:
R1_out_init="$outdir"/"$sample_id"_R1_val_1.fq.gz
```

See also
[this newly added section on renaming files with loops](../week07/w7c_tricks.qmd#renaming-files-with-loops),
though realize that this situation is different:
because you will do the renaming inside the script without a loop.

</details>

### Part C: TrimGalore batch jobs in a loop

After your test-run, it is time to run TrimGalore on all samples by submitting
batch jobs using a loop.

13. Write a `for` loop in your `README.md` to submit a TrimGalore batch job for
    each pair of FASTQ files that you have in your `data` dir.

14. Monitor the batch jobs and when they are done, check that everything went well
    (if it didn't, redo until you get it right).
    In your `README.md`, explain your monitoring and checking process.
    In this case, it is appropriate to keep the Slurm log files:
    move them into a dir `logs` within the TrimGalore output dir.

### Part D: GenAI --- and checking what it tells you

In questions 10-12, you found TrimGalore's color-chemistry option the "old-fashioned"
way: by reading the program's help info.
Now you'll ask a genAI assistant the same question,
which gives you a rare opportunity to judge an AI answer against
a ground truth that you established yourself.

15. Ask a genAI tool of your choice how to deal with the two-color chemistry /
    poly-G problem in TrimGalore.
    You can use your own phrasing, or something like:

    > How can I tell the program TrimGalore that my reads use Illumina two-color chemistry?

    In your `README.md`, document:

    - Which genAI tool (and, if you know it, which model) you used
    - The exact prompt you used
    - The answer you got --- include the relevant code/options,
      and **add a screenshot** of the exchange
      (upload the screenshot to OSC and commit it to your repo)
    - **Your evaluation**: does the option it gave you actually exist in
      `trim_galore --help`?
      Is it the same option you found yourself in question 11?
      If the answer was wrong or partly wrong,
      how confident did the tool _sound_ about it?

    ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
    Whatever you get, follow up at least once:
    for example, ask it to point you to the exact line in the TrimGalore help info
    that documents the option it suggested, and see what happens.
    :::

16. Now pick **one task of your own** related to this assignment that you don't
    know how to do yourself, and ask genAI for help with it.
    Some ideas:

    - Extracting the resource usage (e.g. memory, run time) of all your completed
      batch jobs and collecting it in a small table
    - Checking all your Slurm log files at once for signs that a job failed
    - Counting the reads in each trimmed FASTQ file

    Run the code you get, check that it does what you think it does,
    and document the same items as above
    (tool, prompt, answer, whether it worked, and your own evaluation).
    A screenshot is not required here.

::: callout-warning
#### Remember: you own the answer
For both questions, you are graded on your **evaluation** of the genAI output,
not on whether the tool happened to give a good answer.
A well-documented trial in which you caught the AI being wrong
is worth full points.
:::
